activities.caption: pair each job with the family that does it
activities.name: bmJobMatch

config.prompt: The family predicts the job — pair them:
config.why: Four families do all the work: the bread was mostly carbohydrate, the butter almost entirely fat, the egg white mostly protein — and your body is built from the same four.

activities.caption: file the molecules by their element giveaway
activities.name: bmElementBuckets

config.prompt: The elements tell the families apart. File each molecule:
config.why: Carbohydrates and fats hold carbon, hydrogen and oxygen; proteins add nitrogen (and usually a pinch of sulfur); DNA adds phosphorus — 'no nitrogen, not a protein' is a rule that reliable.

activities.anchor: assembled from small repeating units, like a wall built from
activities.caption: fill the blanks — one brick per family
activities.name: bmBricksCloze

config.text: Every big molecule in this lesson is assembled from small repeating units: starch, glycogen and cellulose are all chains of one brick, the sugar %%0%%. Proteins are chains of %%1%%. Fats are built from %%2%% and glycerol, and DNA from %%3%%.
config.hint: Identical bricks, different walls — enzymes join them and split them apart all day long.

activities.caption: call the magnitude — your glycogen tank
activities.name: bmGlycogenEstimate

config.prompt: Your liver and muscles bank glycogen — roughly how many grams do they hold, all told?
config.why: About 400–500 g — roughly enough fuel to reach a marathon's halfway mark, which is why the wall hits there.
config.context: Glycogen is the animal version of starch, branched more heavily so glucose can be snapped off quickly from many ends.

activities.anchor: The order of the beads is the
activities.caption: stack the four structure levels
activities.name: bmLevelsOrder

config.prompt: From bead order to docking chains — put the levels in order:
items: Primary — the order of the beads (amino acids)
Secondary — hydrogen bonds coil the chain into helices and sheets
Tertiary — the side groups pack it into a precise 3-D shape
Quaternary — separate chains dock together, like haemoglobin's four
config.why: The shape is the job: an active site's pocket, keratin's fibre, haemoglobin's gripper — each level adds organisation without adding ingredients.

activities.caption: true or false — shapes under stress
activities.name: bmDenatureJudge

statements.s: A boiled egg never unboils because heat has shaken the proteins' weak bonds loose and the shapes have unravelled.
statements.why: Denaturation — heat, or the wrong pH, undoes the fold.

statements.s: Cooling the boiled egg back down restores the original proteins.
statements.why: The unravelled tangle does not re-fold — denaturation at the pan's temperature is for keeps.

statements.s: A fever approaching 41 °C is dangerous because your enzymes are nearing the edge of their shapes.
statements.why: Their weak bonds begin to slip — the machinery family is temperature-sensitive.

statements.s: Only heat can denature a protein; pH has no effect on shape.
statements.why: The wrong pH shakes the same weak bonds loose — pH is the measure of how acid something is.

activities.caption: same family, two shapes — drag from butter to olive oil
activities.name: bmSatCompare

config.prompt: Saturated vs unsaturated — drag the divider across the food label:

before.label: saturated
before.text: No carbon–carbon double bonds: straight chains pack tightly — solid butter and lard, the kind associated with raising blood cholesterol.

after.label: unsaturated
after.text: Kinks at the double bonds keep chains from packing: olive oil and fish oils stay liquid — the 'healthier' side of the label.

config.why: One bond geometry, two room-temperature fates — and cold-adapted fish make more unsaturated tails to stay flexible in frigid water.

activities.anchor: A few habits keep the tests honest
activities.caption: run the lab — choose the technique
activities.name: bmTestHabitBranch

config.root: Five food tests on the bench, one sample tray. The habits are what keep the results honest — choose your moves.

start.text: First decision — how do you run Benedict's?

choices.label: Water bath at about 80 °C
choices.feedback: Real heat — the only test of the five that needs it.

choices.label: Naked flame directly on the tube
choices.feedback: The habit list says never — heating must be a bath, not a flame.

choices.label: Skip the heating to save time
choices.feedback: Without heat the colour never develops — sucrose stays blue and so does everything else.

bath.text: Benedict's is heating. Now the biuret reagent — how?

choices.label: Drop by drop
choices.feedback: The honest way — colour develops cleanly.

choices.label: All in at once
choices.feedback: It can give a false cloudiness that mimics a result.

flame.text: Back to the water bath — a naked flame on the tube is the habit the list forbids.

cold.text: No heat, no brick-red — the reducing sugars would never show. Heat it properly and read again.

biuret-ok.text: One more habit: run distilled water through all five tests as a negative control — it should fail every one.

biuret-bad.text: False cloudiness — a result you cannot trust. Drop by drop, and repeat.

config.why: The ethanol emulsion test works only if the sample truly dissolves in the ethanol first — and the sports bar that passes all four has told you more than the wrapper's marketing.
